family: two-block transfer with a tail counter
summary: Two long blocks of pairs 01: every visit of the left end takes 3 pairs from the left block and adds about 6.6 to the right one, paced by a short tail that runs in one of four cycles; when the left block is empty the right one takes its place (rounds grow 2.06 to 2.2-fold). It never halts: a closed set of 1,144 round-end classes (62 tails, the block size by its remainder) is proved in Lean by a symbolic executor with a soundness proof, its runs evaluated by native_decide.
title: What is known about 1RB0RD_1RC0LF_1LA0LB_---1RE_1LB1RA_0LC0RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RD_1RC0LF_1LA0LB_---1RE_1LB1RA_0LC0RA.
intro: This six-state, two-symbol Turing machine is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. It does not halt when started on a blank tape; the proof is in Lean, with its long computations evaluated by compiled code. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: It does not halt (Lean theorem nonhalt, level native). The run is a sequence of rounds. At the end of a round the tape is 01001000 (01)^B T with a big block of B pairs and a short tail T. There are 1,144 classes of such tapes (one of 62 tails, B = r0 + m·x with m = 27, 45, 48 or 66 and r0 ≥ 20,000) such that every tape of a class ends its next round in a class again; the real run enters the set at B = 28,531.

In Lean, a symbolic executor whose every move is proved to be a run of the machine (kernel) runs one round for each class with x free, and the arrival from blank tape; a second proved test shows that every round end announced lies in a class. The 1,144 rounds (133 million executor moves), the arrival and the six cycle rules are evaluated by native_decide, so the result rests on the Lean kernel and the Lean compiler. Step counts are computed by the simulators (trusted), not part of the Lean statement. Tapes of the same shape with a slightly different tail do halt, so the set cannot be widened to all tails.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 38,989 cells have been visited and 19,487 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.498). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.478).

claims.title: Sweeps over the long blocks
claims.text: Eight shift rules, for every number n of words and every surrounding tape. The five sweeps of one visit of the left end, three pairs at a time: 1 C>(010101)^n → (011001)^n 1 C> (14n steps); (011001)^n A>110 → A>110 (010101)^n (22n); 1 B>(010101)^n → (010110)^n 1 B> (14n); (010110)^n B>000 → B>000 (010101)^n (22n); (011001)^n F>0 → F>0 (010101)^n (22n). And three earlier ones (f_left, b_right, e_right).

claims.title: The machine does not halt
claims.text: From blank tape the machine never reaches a halting configuration: nonhalt : ¬ HaltsFromBlank, from nonhalting_of_closed_set with the set of the 1,144 classes and the three claims below. Axioms used: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound and 16 compiled evaluations (native_decide): the arrival, the start node's class, eight chunks of classes, six cycle rules.

claims.title: The machine does not halt: a second proof, in Coq (busycoq)
claims.text: The same argument, ported to Coq on top of busycoq's definitions: nonhalt : ~ halts tm c0. The symbolic executor is proved sound against busycoq's step, and all runs are evaluated inside Coq's kernel by vm_compute; Print Assumptions nonhalt reports no axioms. Clean build with Coq 8.18.0: about 2.5 min.

claims.title: A closed set of round ends implies that it never halts
claims.text: If the run from blank tape reaches a round end A> 01001000 (01)^B T that belongs to a set S, and every round end in S reaches a round end in S after at least one step, then the machine does not halt. Its two hypotheses are proved by the replay below.

claims.title: A symbolic executor and the two class tests, proved sound
claims.text: The executor of 1RB0RC_0RC1RC_0LD0RA_1LE0LF_0LA1LC_---1LA, adapted: tapes of cells and blocks (w)^n with n = c + a·x; shift rules with a carried word, one to three copies at a time; one machine step; at each arrival of state A at the left end a re-bracketing and a cycle rule applied N times, where N may itself be a count N0 + q·x (the subtraction is checked coefficient by coefficient). Any step that would depend on x fails. Theorems: whatever the executor does, the machine does, for every x (run_sound); a class whose run ends at the announced round end does so for every x, in at least one step (clsRun_sound); the coverage test, a finite check over one period of the remainders, implies that every announced B lies in a listed class (covers_sound); a list that passes both is closed (closed_of_checks). The 15 shift rules are proved by evaluation in the kernel.

claims.title: Six cycle rules of the tail, for all values of their counts
claims.text: Each rule says: this tape 110 (01)^a 000 (01)^b T with a = a0 + 3x, b = b0 + 3y comes back, 18 to 44 visits of the left end later, with a smaller by 27 to 66 and b larger by 57 to 141, for all x and y. Each is one run of the executor without cycle rules (9,143 to 25,749 moves), evaluated by native_decide.

claims.title: Blank tape reaches the round end with B = 28,531
claims.text: 527,489 moves of the executor from blank tape end at 01001000 (01)^28531 T with the tail of the certificate, and that round end is in a class of the list (arrive_ok, start_ok, native_decide).

claims.title: The 1,144 classes are closed under one round
claims.text: For each class (tail T, B = r0 + m·x) the executor runs one round with x free (60,000 to 231,000 moves, 132,636,430 in all) and ends at the round end with tail T' and B' = k + c·x of the certificate; every such B' lies in a listed class. So every round end of the set reaches a round end of the set in at least one step. Eight native_decide evaluations of 143 classes each, 35 to 56 s each.

claims.title: The tail cycles
claims.text: Within a round the tape is 010 (01)^a 000 (01)^b T. After a start-up the tail T repeats with a fixed period: 15 visits of the left end (a − 45, b + 99; three different tails), 16 visits (a − 48, b + 99), 22 visits (a − 66, b + 141) or 9 visits (a − 27, b + 57). Each cycle is established by one symbolic run with a and b free (steps affine in both) and re-checked on numbers.

claims.title: The closed set: how it was found, step counts
claims.text: A class is a tail T (62 of them) and a remainder of B (modulo 66: 682 classes; 45: 300; 48: 144; 27: 18), with B ≥ 20,000. For each class one symbolic round with B = r + m·x, x free, ends at 01001000 (01)^B' T' with B' = k + c·x (c = 141, 99 or 57, k ≥ 41,224); every remainder B' can have lies in a class again. The simulator refuses any step whose outcome depends on x. closure.py check re-runs all classes and tests the coverage independently of the search (5 minutes). That the set is closed is now a Lean theorem (above); this tool found it and supplies the step polynomials.

claims.title: The real run enters the closed set: step count, later rounds
claims.text: That blank tape reaches the round end with B = 28,531 is a Lean theorem (above). Computed: from blank tape the run is at the round end with B = 28,531 after 2,340,515,329 steps (the plain C simulator gives the same step), in the class B = 19 mod 66 of its tail. The next 1,302 rounds (B up to 437 digits), computed with numbers, agree with their classes: next tail, next B and the number of steps, all exact; 684 of the classes and all 62 tails occur.

claims.title: Checks of the simulator
claims.text: Five classes at x = 0 and x = 1 against a bit-level simulator (4.1 to 4.3 · 10<sup>9</sup> steps each): state, head position, tape and step count exact. 12 defects injected into the certificate and 8 into the simulator (wrong rule increments, rules without lower bound, wrong number of rule applications, three changed transitions, a class claimed for too coarse a remainder): all 20 reported.

claims.title: Nearby tapes that halt
claims.text: The same shape with another tail can halt: of the tails that differ from one of the 62 by one pair 10 in one block (a sample, 1,141 classes), 5 classes halt for every B, for example tail 000010101010101010101010000101010100001010101010101010101010101110000101 with B = 20,002 + 3x halts after 815,565 + 122x steps (confirmed bit by bit at three values). The other 1,136 fall into the closed set after one round. Other remainders of B for the 62 tails (a sample, 1,722 classes) all fall into the closed set; none halts.

claims.title: Independent check of the closed set
claims.text: A second accelerated simulator written from scratch, without the first tool's engine (verify/accel.cpp, validated against plain simulation up to 4.4·109 steps), confirms the arrival from blank tape at step 2,340,515,329 and, for every one of the 1,144 classes, four members (the two smallest, one B near 106, one near 1011) plus 7,000 random members: no halt, the next round end is exactly the predicted tail, B and step count, and lies in a listed class. 0 mismatches; the five neighbouring tails said to halt do halt. It samples B; that every B of a class behaves so is the Lean theorem closed_set.

explainer.lede: It never halts, and Lean proves it. Two long blocks on this machine's tape act like two buckets: at every visit of the left end a little is poured from the left one into the right one, which grows about twice as fast as the left one shrinks. When the left one is empty the right one takes its place. A short stretch at the right end, the tail, decides how much is poured; at the end of a round it is always one of 62 words, and from none of them does the machine stop.

facts.text: Lean theorem nonhalt; the rounds of 1,144 classes evaluated by compiled code.
The symbolic executor that runs the rounds, and the test that the set is closed, are proved sound in Lean.
A closed set of round ends (62 tails, the block size by its remainder); none reaches the halting transition.
Of the real run, block sizes up to 437 digits, agree with the classes exactly.
Found among nearby tapes with a slightly different tail: the shape alone does not prevent a halt.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.498). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.478).
After 109 steps the tape spans 38,989 cells (7,943 left of the start, 18,839 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Two blocks and a tail
html:
Seen at the moments when the head (in state A) arrives at the left end, the tape is always

010 (01)^a 000 (01)^b T

Here (01)^a means the pair 01 written a times. The left block has a pairs, the big block has b pairs, and T, the tail, is a short word made of a few small blocks of pairs separated by 000 or 111. Example, step 9,932,715,748: a = 2,110, b = 56,419, and the tail has blocks of 4, 13, 16 and 20 pairs.

One visit: the head crosses the whole tape to the right and back, twice. On the way it takes exactly 3 pairs from the left block, and the tail changes a little: its small blocks shrink by 3 pairs each, a block that is used up merges into its neighbour, and from time to time a block is absorbed into the big block. The five crossings of the two long blocks are proved in Lean for blocks of any length.

sections.heading: The tail runs in a cycle
html: The tail does not grow. After a start-up of some dozens of visits it repeats with a fixed period, and in one period fixed amounts leave the left block and enter the big block. Four such cycles occur:

visits in a periodleft blockbig blockratio
15 (three variants)−45 pairs+99 pairs2.2
16−48+992.06
22−66+1412.14
9−27+572.11

Each line was established by running the machine symbolically: the two block sizes are left as unknowns, and the simulator stops if any step would depend on their values. A run that comes back to the same tail is therefore valid for all sizes at once.

sections.heading: When the left block is empty
html:
A round ends when the left block is down to one pair: the tape is then

01001000 (01)^B T

and during the next two visits the big block (B pairs) becomes the new left block, of B + 3 pairs, with a new small big block. So each round is 2.06 to 2.2 times longer than the one before. Sizes B at the round ends: 586, 1,291, 2,827, 6,280, 12,967, 28,531, …

What the next round end looks like depends on two things only: the tail T, and at which point of its cycle the tail is when the left block runs out. The second is decided by the remainder of B when divided by the amount a period eats (45, 48, 66 or 27). The size of B beyond that plays no role, and that is what makes a finite analysis possible.

sections.heading: A closed set of 1,144 classes
html: Call a class all round ends with a given tail T and a given remainder of B (and B at least 20,000). For one class the symbolic simulator runs one whole round with B = r + m·x, where x is an unknown. The result is the next round end: a new tail T' and a new size B' = k + c·x. Whatever x is, B' has one of a few remainders; all of them are put on the list of classes to examine. Nothing about x is remembered, so the list over-counts what the real run can do.

Starting from the round end the real run reaches after 2,340,515,329 steps (B = 28,531), this search stops by itself: 62 tails, 1,144 classes, and every class leads only to classes already on the list. In none of the 1,144 symbolic rounds does the machine reach its halting transition (state D reading 0). So the machine never halts.
The remainders are not a hidden Collatz problem here: the search never asks which remainder comes next in the real run, it accepts all of them.

sections.heading: What this rests on
html: The closed set was found by our own symbolic simulator. It is now also a Lean proof: a second program of the same kind (a symbolic executor: it crosses whole blocks at once and applies a proved cycle many times in one go, a number of times that may depend on the unknown x) is written in Lean and proved correct once: whatever it does, the machine does, for every x. Lean then runs it on each of the 1,144 classes with x unknown, 133 million moves in all, and on the run from blank tape, and checks by a proved test that every round end it arrives at is on the list. Those runs are done by compiled code (native_decide), the one thing trusted beyond Lean's kernel.
What was done before that to test the first simulator, and still supports the step counts quoted here:

• 1,302 consecutive rounds of the real run, with block sizes up to 437 digits, were compared with the classes: next tail, next size and number of steps agree exactly.
  • Ten symbolic rounds were replayed cell by cell by a plain simulator (about 4 billion steps each): same tape, same head position, same step count.
  • 20 deliberate errors were planted in the certificate and in the simulator; the checker reported all 20.
  • A separate checker re-runs all classes and tests that the set is closed without using the search.

Lean's kernel alone proves the five sweeps for blocks of any length, the executor's correctness, and the last step of the argument: a closed set of round ends that the run enters implies that it never halts.

sections.heading: Nearby tapes do halt
html: The shape 01001000 (01)^B T alone does not keep the machine running. Take one of the 62 tails and make one of its small blocks one pair longer or shorter: of 1,141 such classes tried, 1,136 fall back into the closed set after one round, but 5 halt, for every size B. One of them, checked cell by cell: with the tail 0000 (10)^10 000 (10)^4 000 (10)^12 111 0000 101 (the last block has 12 pairs; the real run has this tail with 11) and B = 20,002 the machine halts after 815,565 steps.

So the argument really needs the exact list of 62 tails; a statement about all tails would be false. Other remainders of B for the 62 tails are harmless: all 1,722 classes tried fall into the closed set.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.
